content: Oral 5-aminosalicylic acid (5-ASA), also known as mesalazine or mesalamine, was developed to retain the therapeutic benefits of sulfasalazine (SASP) while minimizing its adverse effects. Previous research demonstrated that 5-ASA is more effective than placebo in maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis (UC), but it is less effective than SASP. This updated review re-evaluates the efficacy, dose-responsiveness, and safety of oral 5-ASA compared to placebo, SASP, or other 5-ASA formulations, as well as the effectiveness of once-daily dosing versus conventional dosing regimens. A systematic search of the literature was conducted on June 11, 2019, using MEDLINE, Embase, and the Cochrane Library. Additional sources, such as review articles and conference proceedings, were also examined. Randomized controlled trials with a minimum treatment duration of six months were included. These studies compared oral 5-ASA with placebo, SASP, or other 5-ASA formulations, as well as once-daily versus conventional dosing regimens. The primary outcome was the failure to maintain clinical or endoscopic remission. Secondary outcomes included adherence to medication, adverse events (AEs), serious adverse events (SAEs), and withdrawals due to AEs. The review included 44 studies with a total of 9,967 participants. Most studies had a low risk of bias, although 10 studies were identified as having a high risk of bias. Seven of these were single-blind, and three were open-label. Efficacy of 5-ASA versus placebo: 5-ASA was found to be more effective than placebo in maintaining clinical or endoscopic remission. Approximately 37% of participants receiving 5-ASA relapsed within six to 12 months, compared to 55% of those receiving placebo (risk ratio [RR] 0.68, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.61 to 0.76; high-certainty evidence). Serious adverse events (SAEs) occurred in 1% of participants in the 5-ASA group and 2% in the placebo group (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.84; low-certainty evidence). There was likely little or no difference in the overall incidence of adverse events between the two groups (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.18; moderate-certainty evidence). Efficacy of 5-ASA versus SASP: SASP was more effective than 5-ASA in maintaining remission. Approximately 48% of participants receiving 5-ASA relapsed within six to 18 months, compared to 43% of those receiving SASP (RR 1.14, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.27; high-certainty evidence). Data on adherence and SAEs were not reported for this comparison. There was likely little or no difference in the incidence of adverse events between the two groups (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.40; moderate-certainty evidence). Once-daily versus conventional dosing of 5-ASA: There was little or no difference in remission rates between once-daily and conventional dosing regimens. Approximately 37% of participants in the once-daily group relapsed over 12 months, compared to 39% in the conventional-dosing group (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.01; high-certainty evidence). Adherence rates were also similar, with 10% of participants in the once-daily group failing to adhere to their medication regimen compared to 8% in the conventional-dosing group (RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.93; moderate-certainty evidence). SAEs occurred in 3% of participants in the once-daily group and 2% in the conventional-dosing group (RR 1.20, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.87; moderate-certainty evidence). There was little or no difference in the overall incidence of adverse events between the two dosing regimens (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.04; high-certainty evidence). Comparison of different 5-ASA formulations: There may be little or no difference in efficacy between different 5-ASA formulations. Approximately 44% of participants in one 5-ASA group relapsed within six to 18 months, compared to 41% in the comparator 5-ASA group (RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.28; low-certainty evidence). Conclusions: High-certainty evidence supports the superiority of 5-ASA over placebo for maintaining remission in UC. However, SASP is more effective than 5-ASA for this purpose. There is likely little or no difference in the incidence of commonly reported adverse events, such as flatulence, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, and dyspepsia, between 5-ASA and placebo or between 5-ASA and SASP. Once-daily dosing of 5-ASA appears to be as effective and safe as conventional dosing regimens for maintaining remission in quiescent UC.
